documentation.content:
# Dry Bean

This dataset explores morphological differences among seven dry bean varieties and provides a governed multiclass machine-learning model for classifying individual bean samples from numerical shape measurements.

The objective is not only to obtain a predicted class, but also to document the analytical path from understanding the dataset to evaluating a multiclass model on previously unseen data.

## Dataset overview

Each row represents a single dry bean grain described by numerical morphological measurements extracted from images.

| Item | Value |
| --- | ---: |
| Bean samples | 13,611 |
| Source columns | 17 |
| Predictive features | 16 |
| Target | `Class` |
| Target classes | 7 |
| Problem type | Multiclass classification |
| Source | UCI Machine Learning Repository |
| UCI dataset ID | `602` |

The target column is never exposed as a predictive feature.

The seven classes are:

* `BARBUNYA`
* `BOMBAY`
* `CALI`
* `DERMASON`
* `HOROZ`
* `SEKER`
* `SIRA`

The predictive features describe different aspects of bean geometry, including overall size, perimeter, principal-axis dimensions, elongation, convexity, roundness, compactness, and derived shape factors.

## Analytical question

The analysis investigates two related questions:

1. **How do the observed morphological characteristics differ among the seven bean varieties?**
2. **How effectively can those measurements be used to classify previously unseen bean samples?**

The project begins with numerical features already extracted from bean images.

It does not reproduce the original image acquisition, segmentation, or feature-extraction process.

Observed relationships between morphology and bean class should therefore be interpreted as predictive associations within this dataset rather than causal or agronomic effects.

## Data quality and preparation

The source contains 13,611 observations and 16 numerical candidate features.

The preparation process preserves the source dataset without generic imputation, row removal, or automatic outlier deletion.

All 16 validated predictive features remain available to the model.

The governed Atlas execution contract uses a stratified split with random seed `42`:

| Partition | Approximate share | Purpose |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Train | 70% | Model fitting |
| Validation | 15% | Governed model evaluation |
| Test | 15% | Final holdout evaluation |

In the active Atlas run, validation contains 2,040 rows and the final test partition contains 2,044 rows.

The test partition is kept outside model fitting and is evaluated only during finalization.

Repeated feature profiles may occur in the source. Because the dataset provides no observation identifier, exact equality between feature profiles is not treated as proof that two records represent the same physical grain.

## Class distribution

The seven classes are not equally represented.

`DERMASON` is the most frequent class, while `BOMBAY` is the least frequent.

| Class | Rows | Share |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| SEKER | 2,027 | 14.89% |
| BARBUNYA | 1,322 | 9.71% |
| BOMBAY | 522 | 3.84% |
| CALI | 1,630 | 11.98% |
| DERMASON | 3,546 | 26.05% |
| HOROZ | 1,928 | 14.17% |
| SIRA | 2,636 | 19.37% |

The majority-to-minority support ratio is approximately `6.79`.

![Dry Bean target class distribution](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FabioAguiar/dataset-study-dry-bean/main/docs/images/target_class_distribution.png)

Because class support is unequal, model evaluation does not rely on accuracy alone.

Macro-averaged metrics are especially useful because they give each class equal influence on the aggregate result.

## Key exploratory findings

### Morphological measurements contain strong class information

Several size and shape measurements show substantial univariate association with bean class.

The strongest exploratory associations include:

* `Area`;
* `ConvexArea`;
* `EquivDiameter`;
* `Perimeter`;
* `MinorAxisLength`;
* `MajorAxisLength`.

![Univariate feature-to-target associations](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FabioAguiar/dataset-study-dry-bean/main/docs/images/feature_target_association_ranking.png)

These results show that bean morphology contains substantial information about class identity.

They do not mean that individual features should be interpreted independently or causally.

### The feature space contains substantial structural redundancy

Several morphological measurements are strongly related.

Examples include:

* `Area` and `ConvexArea`;
* `Area` and `EquivDiameter`;
* `Perimeter` and `EquivDiameter`;
* `AspectRatio` and `Eccentricity`;
* `Compactness` and `ShapeFactor3`.

The exploratory analysis identified 21 feature pairs meeting the predefined redundancy-review threshold.

![Numerical feature correlation heatmap](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FabioAguiar/dataset-study-dry-bean/main/docs/images/numerical_feature_correlation_heatmap.png)

Strong correlation does not automatically imply that a feature should be removed.

The complete validated feature set is therefore retained unless later model-selection evidence supports a different policy.

### Some bean classes have overlapping morphological profiles

The seven classes do not occupy completely isolated regions of the feature space.

The exploratory class-profile analysis identified:

* `DERMASON` and `SIRA` as the closest pair by robust central-profile distance;
* `BARBUNYA` and `CALI` as the pair with the greatest mean central IQR overlap.

![Standardized Dry Bean class profiles](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FabioAguiar/dataset-study-dry-bean/main/docs/images/standardized_class_profiles.png)

A two-component PCA projection captures approximately 81.9% of the standardized exploratory variance and provides another view of this overlap.

![Exploratory PCA projection](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FabioAguiar/dataset-study-dry-bean/main/docs/images/class_pca_projection.png)

PCA position and profile overlap are descriptive evidence only. They do not directly estimate classifier error.

## Model selection evidence

The companion Dry Bean study compared several machine-learning families under a stratified multiclass evaluation design:

* Logistic Regression;
* Decision Tree;
* Random Forest;
* HistGradientBoosting.

HistGradientBoosting with all 16 features produced the strongest validation result under the predefined selection policy.

![Validation model comparison](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FabioAguiar/dataset-study-dry-bean/main/docs/images/model_validation_comparison.png)

The study also evaluated feature-policy sensitivity.

Removing `ShapeFactor2` produced only a small decrease in validation macro F1, while removing the broader set of confirmed derived features produced a substantially larger reduction.

![Feature policy sensitivity](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FabioAguiar/dataset-study-dry-bean/main/docs/images/feature_policy_sensitivity.png)

The resulting Atlas execution contract therefore retains all 16 features and freezes a `HistGradientBoostingClassifier` configuration.

Atlas does not perform AutoML or unrestricted model search for this release.

The governed configuration uses:

```text
model family         = hist_gradient_boosting
learning_rate        = 0.05
max_iter             = 250
max_leaf_nodes       = 15
min_samples_leaf     = 40
l2_regularization    = 0.0
class_weight         = None
random_seed          = 42
```

## Active Atlas release evaluation

The active Atlas release is:

`release-20260818-002`

Its governed final holdout evaluation contains 2,044 test observations.

| Metric | Final test |
| --- | ---: |
| **F1 Macro** | **0.9433** |
| Balanced Accuracy | **0.9436** |
| Recall Macro | 0.9436 |
| F1 Weighted | 0.9340 |
| Accuracy | 0.9340 |
| Log Loss ↓ | 0.1942 |

The final per-class recall values show strong performance across all seven classes:

| Class | Recall |
| --- | ---: |
| BARBUNYA | 0.9347 |
| BOMBAY | 1.0000 |
| CALI | 0.9510 |
| DERMASON | 0.9323 |
| HOROZ | 0.9516 |
| SEKER | 0.9441 |
| SIRA | 0.8914 |

`SIRA` is the most difficult class in the final holdout evaluation, but its recall remains approximately 89.1%.

The main residual confusion is concentrated around morphologically related or overlapping classes rather than being distributed uniformly across all seven categories.

These results describe performance under the current governed random-snapshot evaluation. They do not establish temporal or production generalization.

## Understanding the highlighted metrics

### F1 Macro — 0.9433

Macro F1 calculates an F1 score independently for each class and then gives every class equal weight in the final average.

This makes it particularly appropriate for Dry Bean because the seven target classes have unequal support.

A large class such as `DERMASON` therefore does not dominate the metric simply because it contains more observations than a smaller class such as `BOMBAY`.

**Higher values are better.**

F1 Macro is the primary governed evaluation metric for the active Dry Bean execution contract and is therefore the highlighted score in Atlas.

### Balanced Accuracy — 0.9436

Balanced Accuracy averages recall across classes.

For multiclass classification, it helps show whether predictive performance remains distributed across classes rather than being driven primarily by the majority class.

**Higher values are better.**

Although its numerical value is slightly higher than Macro F1, it is a secondary metric in the governed execution contract.

### Accuracy — 0.9340

Accuracy represents the proportion of test observations assigned to the correct bean class.

It provides an intuitive overall measure, but it does not give every class equal influence when class frequencies differ.

For that reason, Accuracy is presented as supporting evidence rather than the primary score.

**Higher values are better.**

The numerical values of different metrics should not be interpreted as directly competing quantities. Each metric describes a different aspect of classification performance.

## Multiclass inference experience

The Atlas inference form receives 16 numerical morphological measurements.

These inputs are organized into four presentation groups:

* size and dimensions;
* proportions and elongation;
* compactness and convexity;
* derived shape factors.

The model produces one predicted class from the seven governed bean classes.

Unlike binary classification, there is no positive class and no positive-class probability.

The result also includes a probability distribution across all seven classes.

The decision strategy is:

`argmax`

This means that the class with the highest model probability is returned as the predicted class.

No binary classification threshold or operational decision threshold is involved.

## What this dataset demonstrates

Dry Bean extends the Atlas educational workflow from binary classification into native multiclass classification.

The project demonstrates:

* dataset understanding and exploratory analysis;
* multiclass target contracts;
* deterministic data preparation;
* stratified train, validation, and test partitions;
* explicit class-order governance;
* multiclass-aware model evaluation;
* macro-averaged performance metrics;
* fixed model configuration;
* final holdout evaluation;
* multiclass probability outputs;
* contract-driven inference.

It therefore provides an important second dataset for validating that Atlas abstractions are not restricted to positive-versus-negative binary prediction problems.

## Limitations

Several important boundaries remain:

* the evaluation is based on a random stratified snapshot rather than a temporal or external validation dataset;
* the model starts from image-derived numerical features rather than raw bean images;
* the original image-acquisition and feature-extraction process is outside the scope of Atlas inference;
* exploratory feature associations do not establish causal or agronomic relationships;
* morphological overlap remains between some classes;
* evaluation on this dataset does not establish performance on beans collected under different imaging equipment, environments, or populations;
* no production monitoring or dataset-drift policy is established by this study;
* the educational evaluation does not establish operational or commercial suitability.

## Responsible interpretation

The evidence supports the following conclusion:

> In this dataset, numerical measurements of bean size and shape provide strong predictive information for distinguishing seven dry bean varieties. The active Atlas release uses a governed HistGradientBoosting multiclass model with all 16 morphological features and achieves a final-test Macro F1 of approximately 0.9433 and Balanced Accuracy of approximately 0.9436. Performance remains strong across all seven classes, although some morphological overlap and residual class confusion remain.

The Atlas inference experience should therefore be interpreted as an interactive representation of a governed multiclass predictive workflow rather than as a universal bean-identification system.
